catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achaz:
Achaz, or Ahaz, was King of Juda, with reign dates variously placed between 748 and 709 BC. What seems certain is that Theglathphalasar's first expedition against Damascus in his story fell in 733 BC and the second in 731. Through idolatry Achaz was conquered first by Rasin of Syria and then by Phacee of Israel. Rasin and Phacee allied to dethrone David's house and make the son of Tabeel king.

The prophet Isaias offered Achaz God's aid with safety for belief and punishment for unbelief. Achaz disbelieved, sought help from Theglathphalasar, and paid rich presents from the temple treasury. The Assyrian took Damascus and afflicted Israel, but reduced Juda to buying its freedom. Unimproved by affliction, Achaz set a Damascus-modelled altar in the temple, and Juda suffered further from Edomites and Philistines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alvarez-de-pa:
Alvarez de Paz, famous Jesuit mystic, was born at Toledo in 1560 and died at Potosí on 17 January 1620. He joined the Society in 1578 and taught at Lima, theology and philosophy both, before rising to Provincial of Peru. He told his confessor that through twenty-five years of distracting work his union with God never broke. Sometimes in sermons he fell into ecstasy and was carried from the pulpit.

Dying at Potosí, he was met by the whole city seeking his blessing, and 100,000 miners stopped work for his obsequies. He reportedly had prophecy's gift and an incorrupt body after death. His three folio treatises, De vita spirituali of 1608, De exterminatione mali of 1613, and De inquisitione pacis of 1611, were widely used in compendiums and translations. Poulain judged his bent philosophical and erudite rather than patiently observant, first using oratio affectiva for affection-led contemplation.
